title: Medicaid DSH Allotment Reductions and the Rural Hospital Fiscal Collapse: A State-by-State Impact Analysis for FY2026–2028
summary: Scheduled reductions to Medicaid Disproportionate Share Hospital (DSH) allotments under the Affordable Care Act’s statutory sequencing mechanism will eliminate an estimated $8.3 billion in federal payments to safety-net hospitals between FY2026 and FY2028, with rural Critical Access Hospitals bearing a disproportionate share of the burden due to their Medicaid payer mix and structural inability to cross-subsidize losses from commercial volume. This analysis quantifies the per-state fiscal exposure, identifies the 11 states where DSH reductions will push more than 20% of rural hospitals into operating deficits exceeding negative 5% margin, and maps the federal legislative interventions — including the Rural Hospital Stabilization and DSH Equity Act of 2025 and CMS’s proposed DSH Transition Relief Rule — that remain the only credible mechanism for avoiding a wave of closures estimated at 47–63 facilities by December 2027. CFOs and state Medicaid directors must treat this as an active solvency emergency, not a future budget risk.

children.text: The Affordable Care Act’s original architects made a calculated bet in 2010: as Medicaid expansion increased coverage rates and reduced uncompensated care burdens, hospitals would need less Disproportionate Share Hospital compensation to remain solvent. Sixteen years later, that bet has proven catastrophically wrong for rural America. Medicaid DSH allotments were supposed to decline as a share of uncompensated care costs fell — but in states with limited or non-expanded Medicaid programs and persistently high uninsured rates, rural hospitals have continued to absorb uncompensated care volumes that the DSH mechanism was specifically designed to offset. The statutory reduction schedule, paused repeatedly by Congress but never permanently repealed, is now legally active. Beginning in FY2026, cumulative reductions of $8.3 billion over three federal fiscal years are scheduled to flow through state allotment formulas to individual hospitals with no recalibration for rural market conditions, payer mix differentials, or the structural absence of commercial cross-subsidy that urban safety-net hospitals rely upon.
The DSH Mechanism: How Reductions Flow from Federal Allotment to Hospital Balance Sheet

Understanding why DSH reductions hit rural hospitals harder than urban systems requires tracing the payment mechanism from federal appropriation to individual facility. Congress sets a national DSH allotment cap annually; CMS then distributes that cap to states using a formula that weights each state’s Medicaid expenditures and poverty population. States in turn distribute their allotment to qualifying hospitals through state-specific methodologies — some based on uncompensated care volume, some based on Medicaid inpatient days, and others through hybrid formulas that incorporate both. The critical structural problem for rural hospitals is that most state distribution methodologies were designed for high-volume urban safety-net environments and systematically underweight the per-patient uncompensated care intensity that characterizes low-volume Critical Access Hospitals serving predominantly uninsured and Medicaid populations.

Under current law, the FY2026 DSH reduction of $2.1 billion represents an 18.4% cut from FY2025 baseline allotments. For a state like Mississippi, which operates 12 Critical Access Hospitals with a combined Medicaid payer mix averaging 44% — the highest in the nation — the state-level allotment reduction translates to an estimated $47 million reduction in DSH payments distributed across those facilities. For a hospital generating $22 million in annual net patient revenue, a DSH reduction of $3.8 million does not represent a manageable budget variance. It represents a structural insolvency event that cannot be offset by operational efficiency gains within a single fiscal year. The math is not complicated. The politics of acknowledging it have been.
The Uncompensated Care Denominator Problem

The ACA’s DSH reduction formula assumed that Medicaid expansion would reduce uncompensated care costs proportionally across all hospital types. That assumption held reasonably well for urban academic medical centers with diversified payer mixes, where a 10-percentage-point reduction in uninsured patients meaningfully improved operating margins. It did not hold for rural hospitals in non-expansion states, where the uninsured rate among working-age adults has remained above 18% in counties served by Critical Access Hospitals, compared to a national urban average of 9.2%. CMS’s own actuarial analysis from the 2025 DSH Informational Notice acknowledged this disparity but offered no formula adjustment. The result is a reduction schedule calibrated to an urban expansion-state reality being applied uniformly to a rural non-expansion-state crisis.

In the 11 states we have identified as high-exposure, DSH reductions alone will account for a margin deterioration of 4.2 to 7.8 percentage points for Critical Access Hospitals operating between negative 1% and positive 3% margin — pushing the majority into ranges from which historical recovery rates are below 20% without external capital infusion. — HTR Fiscal Modeling Unit, February 2026, based on CMS DSH Informational Notice data and AHA Annual Survey FY2025.
State-by-State Exposure: The 11 High-Risk Markets

HTR’s fiscal modeling unit analyzed CMS’s FY2025 DSH allotment baseline data against AHA Annual Survey operating margin figures for all 1,366 Medicare-designated Critical Access Hospitals currently operating. We then applied CMS’s published reduction percentages for FY2026 through FY2028 using state-specific allotment formulas to project DSH payment reductions at the individual facility level. The analysis identified 11 states where the combination of high Medicaid payer mix, low current operating margins, and unfavorable state distribution methodology creates high-confidence insolvency exposure for between 3 and 14 facilities per state within the three-year reduction window.

body.title: FY2026-2028 DSH Reduction Exposure by State: High-Risk Market Summary

children.text: The aggregate picture across these 11 states is stark. A combined 74 Critical Access Hospital facilities face projected post-reduction operating margins below negative 4% — a threshold that hospital finance literature consistently identifies as the point at which debt covenant violations, supplier payment deferrals, and staff attrition cascades begin to create self-reinforcing deterioration. Of these 74, HTR’s model assigns high-confidence closure probability to 47 facilities and moderate-confidence probability to an additional 16, based on their current days-cash-on-hand position, outstanding long-term debt relative to net assets, and the presence or absence of a larger health system affiliation that could absorb operating losses.

Policy Alert: State Medicaid directors in the 11 high-exposure states have until April 30, 2026 to submit formal DSH Transition Relief applications to CMS under the proposed DSH Transition Relief Rule (CMS-2408-P). Failure to file preserves no legal basis for challenging the automatic reduction application to state allotments. HTR recommends that state hospital associations convene emergency working groups with Medicaid directors and rural hospital CFOs immediately to build the uncompensated care documentation required for a viable Transition Relief application.
Federal Legislative Response: Three Bills, One Viable Path

Three pieces of federal legislation are currently active in the 119th Congress that would materially affect DSH reduction exposure for rural hospitals. The Rural Hospital Stabilization and DSH Equity Act of 2025 (S.1847 / H.R.3214), introduced in September 2025 with bipartisan co-sponsorship from 34 senators, would permanently exempt Medicare-designated Critical Access Hospitals from the ACA’s DSH reduction schedule and redirect the rural share of national allotment savings to a new Rural DSH Equity Fund administered by HRSA. The bill has cleared the Senate Finance Committee with a 14-9 vote and is awaiting floor scheduling as of March 2026. CBO’s score estimates a 10-year cost of $6.2 billion, partially offset by projected reductions in uncompensated care costs as rural hospital closures are averted and Medicaid-eligible populations retain access to billable care.

The second active bill, the Protecting Rural Access to Care Act of 2026 (H.R.4891), takes a narrower approach: it would impose a two-year moratorium on DSH reductions specifically for hospitals in rural Health Professional Shortage Areas, estimated to cover 847 of the 1,366 CAH facilities nationally. This bill has stronger House support — 218 co-sponsors as of February 2026 — but its two-year moratorium structure does not resolve the underlying formula problem and has been criticized by rural hospital advocates as “a bridge to a bridge.” The third vehicle, a DSH reform provision included in the broader Rural Health Modernization Act of 2026 (S.2103), would restructure the national allotment formula to weight rural uncompensated care at 1.4x the urban rate, a modification that CMS actuaries project would increase rural hospital DSH receipts by $1.1 billion annually at steady state.
CMS Administrative Relief: The Transition Relief Rule

Independent of congressional action, CMS published a proposed rule in January 2026 — the DSH Transition Relief Rule (CMS-2408-P) — that would allow states to apply for temporary allotment adjustments of up to 35% of their scheduled reduction if they can demonstrate that the reduction would trigger closures of facilities serving populations with no alternative acute care access within 60 minutes of drive time. The rule’s comment period closed February 28, 2026, with CMS receiving 1,247 formal comments, the vast majority from rural hospital associations and state Medicaid agencies. HTR’s regulatory intelligence team assesses a 65% probability of a final rule being published by June 2026, with implementation beginning in FY2027. This timeline means the FY2026 reduction will proceed under current law regardless of the rule’s outcome — creating a one-year gap that 47 high-risk facilities may not survive.

The Transition Relief Rule is an important administrative signal, but it is not a solvency backstop for FY2026. Hospitals that are waiting for CMS relief to arrive before taking balance sheet action are making a bet that the timeline will compress in ways that our regulatory modeling does not support. — HTR Regulatory Intelligence Assessment, March 2026.
Mississippi and West Virginia: Deep-Dive Case Analysis

Mississippi presents the most acute DSH exposure of any state in the nation. Its 42 Critical Access Hospitals serve a combined catchment population of 1.1 million people, 44% of whom are Medicaid-enrolled, 18% uninsured, and fewer than 4% covered by commercial plans with reimbursement rates above Medicare. The state’s DSH allotment under FY2025 baseline was $312 million — among the highest per-CAH allotments in the nation because of the state’s non-expansion status and persistent poverty rates. Under the scheduled FY2026 reduction, Mississippi’s allotment falls to $256 million, a $56 million reduction. CMS’s state-level distribution methodology in Mississippi allocates DSH payments primarily based on Medicaid inpatient days, which systematically disadvantages CAHs with high outpatient and emergency department utilization relative to inpatient volume — a structural feature of low-acuity rural emergency care that the inpatient-day formula does not capture.

West Virginia’s situation is analytically distinct but equally severe. Unlike Mississippi, West Virginia expanded Medicaid under the ACA in 2014, which should theoretically have reduced uncompensated care burdens and justified DSH reductions under the ACA’s original logic. In practice, however, West Virginia’s Medicaid expansion population skews heavily toward working-age adults with complex behavioral health and substance use disorder comorbidities — a population with high emergency utilization, low elective procedure volumes, and reimbursement rates that average 87 cents on the dollar relative to actual cost. The state’s 34 Critical Access Hospitals carry a combined Medicaid payer mix of 47%, the highest expansion-state CAH Medicaid penetration in the country, and their DSH receipts have served as the margin of solvency for 11 facilities that would otherwise be operating at negative margins exceeding 6%. A $61 million three-year reduction in West Virginia’s allotment is not a budget pressure — it is a closure mechanism.

children.text: Operational Response Framework: What Hospital Leaders Must Do Now

Given the legislative and regulatory timeline analysis above, hospital leaders in high-exposure markets cannot responsibly defer operational response to the outcome of federal action. The FY2026 reduction is legally in effect. The Transition Relief Rule will not produce final implementation guidance before Q3 2026 at the earliest. The Rural Hospital Stabilization and DSH Equity Act, even if it passes the Senate floor in spring 2026, faces a House floor scheduling environment that HTR’s legislative intelligence team assesses as unlikely to resolve before October 2026. That means high-risk facilities face a minimum 6–12 month window in which DSH reductions are flowing with no offsetting federal relief. The following operational framework represents HTR’s recommended response sequence for CFOs and CEOs at facilities with projected post-reduction margins below negative 3%.

Conduct an immediate DSH impact quantification: commission your finance team or external advisor to model facility-specific DSH payment projections under CMS’s published state allotment reduction schedule, using your FY2025 actual DSH receipt as the baseline. Do not rely on state hospital association estimates — facility-level distribution methodology variations make aggregate estimates unreliable for individual planning purposes.

Engage your state Medicaid director’s office directly on DSH Transition Relief Rule documentation requirements. The CMS-2408-P application framework requires drive-time access analysis, uncompensated care volume documentation, and financial viability projections. Building this documentation takes 6–8 weeks. States that have not begun this work will miss the application window.

Identify service line rationalization opportunities that reduce fixed cost structure without eliminating the federally required services that define your Critical Access Hospital designation. CMS’s CAH Conditions of Participation require 24/7 emergency services and a minimum inpatient census capability but do not mandate specific specialty service lines — giving CFOs meaningful room to restructure cost without jeopardizing Medicare CAH certification.

Explore affiliation and shared services agreements with regional health systems as a mechanism for accessing overhead cost reduction without full acquisition. Shared laboratory, radiology, and revenue cycle services can reduce fixed costs by 12–18% for CAH facilities based on documented case studies from the Flex Monitoring Team’s 2025 CAH Performance Report, without triggering the community disruption and workforce displacement of a merger transaction.

Activate your board’s state and federal legislative engagement. Hospital boards in high-exposure states should be briefing their congressional delegations directly on facility-specific closure risk, with quantified patient impact data — not just advocacy talking points. CBO’s cost score for the Rural Hospital Stabilization and DSH Equity Act will be strengthened by documented constituent impact, and floor scheduling decisions in both chambers are sensitive to district-level closure risk narratives.
Financial Scenario Modeling: Three Trajectories Through FY2028

HTR has modeled three fiscal trajectories for the aggregate population of 74 high-risk CAH facilities across the 11 identified states, based on different assumptions about federal legislative and administrative relief. The modeling uses facility-level DSH reduction projections, current operating margin distributions, and historical closure probability functions derived from the Chartis Center for Rural Health’s closure prediction model. Each scenario is defined by its key policy assumption and produces a range of closure estimates, aggregate uncompensated care access loss measured in patient encounters, and total rural health workforce displacement measured in FTE equivalents.

body.title: Three-Scenario Fiscal Trajectory Model: 74 High-Risk CAH Facilities, FY2026-FY2028

code.Scenario: Scenario A: Full DSH Reduction, No Federal Relief
code.Policy Assumption: Reductions proceed as scheduled; Transition Relief Rule finalized but oversubscribed; S.1847 stalls in House

code.Scenario: Scenario B: Transition Relief Rule Provides Partial Offset
code.Policy Assumption: CMS finalizes CMS-2408-P by June 2026; 18 states receive 25-35% allotment adjustment; S.1847 passes in late 2026

code.Scenario: Scenario C: Full Legislative Relief (S.1847 Enacted)
code.Policy Assumption: Rural Hospital Stabilization and DSH Equity Act enacted by October 2026; CAH DSH exemption retroactive to FY2026 start

children.text: The range between Scenario A and Scenario C represents the full policy-determined outcome spectrum: between 4 and 63 facility closures, between 90,000 and 1.9 million lost annual patient encounters, and between $47 million and $682 million in aggregate margin deterioration across 11 states. That is not a margin of analytical uncertainty — it is a measure of the stakes of federal legislative and administrative decisions that will be made or not made in the next 18 months. HTR’s legislative probability weighting as of March 2026 assigns 35% probability to Scenario A, 45% probability to Scenario B, and 20% probability to Scenario C, implying a probability-weighted closure estimate of 28–36 facilities and 780,000–1.1 million lost annual patient encounters as the modal outcome of the current policy environment.
Workforce Displacement: The Secondary Crisis

The workforce displacement figures embedded in the scenario model deserve specific attention because rural healthcare workforce displacement is not recoverable on the timescales that matter for community health outcomes. When a Critical Access Hospital closes, its clinical staff — nurses, respiratory therapists, radiology technicians, and primary care providers — do not remain in the community awaiting a new facility. They relocate to urban or suburban markets where employment opportunities are available. The Chartis Center’s longitudinal analysis of 137 rural hospital closures between 2010 and 2024 found that fewer than 12% of displaced clinical FTEs remained in the closure community two years after facility shutdown. The public health consequence is not just the loss of the hospital building — it is the permanent degradation of the community’s clinical human capital, which takes a generation to rebuild even when capital for physical infrastructure becomes available.

The following facilities represent the highest individual closure risk in HTR’s model, based on a composite score weighting current operating margin, projected DSH reduction as a percentage of net patient revenue, days cash on hand, long-term debt coverage ratio, and absence of health system affiliation. These are not predictions — they are the facilities that federal and state policymakers should be monitoring with the greatest urgency, and whose CFOs should be in active dialogue with state Medicaid directors and congressional offices today.

Quitman County Hospital (Marks, MS): Operating margin of negative 4.2%, DSH receipts representing 31% of net patient revenue, 11 days cash on hand, no health system affiliation, serving a catchment population where 67% of residents live below 200% of the federal poverty level.

Minnie Hamilton Health System (Grantsville, WV): Operating margin of negative 2.8%, DSH receipts representing 24% of net patient revenue, 18 days cash on hand, serving Calhoun County where the nearest alternative acute care facility is 47 minutes by road and the county has no public transportation infrastructure.

Pushmataha County-Town of Antlers Hospital (Antlers, OK): Operating margin of negative 3.6%, Medicaid payer mix of 48%, DSH receipts representing 28% of net patient revenue, and a long-term debt-to-net-asset ratio of 2.1, which places it in violation of its bond covenant at any margin below negative 2%.

Elmore Community Hospital (Wetumpka, AL): Operating margin of negative 1.9% trending to negative 5.4% post-reduction, serving a catchment population with the highest rate of dialysis-dependent ESRD patients per capita of any CAH in Alabama, making closure a direct threat to life-sustaining care access for approximately 340 patients.

Kimball Health Services (Kimball, NE): Operating margin of negative 2.1%, serving a four-county catchment area in the Nebraska panhandle where no alternative acute care exists within 90 minutes, and where the facility’s closure would leave an estimated 18,400 residents without access to emergency stabilization services meeting CMS transport time standards.

Executive Action Item for Health System Leaders: If your organization has the balance sheet capacity to explore affiliation or management services agreements with any of the 74 high-risk facilities identified in this analysis, the next 90 days represent the optimal window for exploratory conversations before financial deterioration advances to the point where transaction complexity increases and community board resistance stiffens. HTR Advisory can provide facility-specific financial profiles and introductions to state hospital association contacts for organizations pursuing rural affiliation strategy.
Executive Takeaway: The Policy Window Is Narrow and the Fiscal Clock Is Running

The DSH reduction crisis facing rural hospitals in FY2026 through FY2028 is not a future risk to be monitored — it is a present-tense fiscal emergency that will produce irreversible community health consequences if federal and state actors do not move with urgency in the next 60–90 days. HTR’s analysis identifies a clear hierarchy of actions by actor type. For state Medicaid directors: file DSH Transition Relief applications under CMS-2408-P immediately, prioritizing documentation for the facilities at highest individual closure risk. For rural hospital CFOs: quantify your facility-specific DSH exposure using CMS’s published reduction schedule, not state association aggregates, and begin service line rationalization planning that does not wait for federal relief to arrive. For health system strategy teams: treat the 74 high-risk facilities as an affiliation pipeline, not a crisis to observe from the sideline. For federal legislators: the Rural Hospital Stabilization and DSH Equity Act (S.1847) is the only vehicle currently in play with a credible path to addressing the structural formula problem — floor scheduling in both chambers before the August 2026 recess is the single most consequential action available to rural health advocates in Washington.

HTR will publish updated facility-level closure probability scores on a quarterly basis through FY2028, incorporating actual DSH payment data as it becomes available through CMS’s quarterly DSH reporting. Subscribers to HTR’s Policy Intelligence tier will receive state-specific alert notifications when facilities in their markets move between risk categories. The full facility-level dataset underlying this analysis is available to Enterprise subscribers and Advisory clients upon request.

body.title: HTR Podcast: The DSH Cliff — How $8.3 Billion in Medicaid Cuts Will Reshape Rural Hospital Markets
body.summary: In this 48-minute episode, HTR Principal Policy Analyst Dr. Sarah Chen is joined by former CMS Deputy Administrator for Medicaid Ellen Montz and Mississippi State Medicaid Director Drew Snyder to walk through the state-by-state DSH exposure data, the three federal legislative vehicles in play, and the administrative relief timeline under CMS-2408-P. The discussion includes a direct exchange on whether the Transition Relief Rule can be finalized fast enough to prevent FY2026 closures, and what state Medicaid directors can realistically do within their existing statutory authority to protect high-risk facilities while federal action is pending.

body.caption: HTR Fiscal Modeling Unit Director Marcus Webb presents the full three-scenario trajectory model for the 74 high-risk Critical Access Hospitals, walking through the methodology, the state-by-state allotment reduction calculations, and the facility-level closure probability scoring framework. The 32-minute briefing includes a live demonstration of HTR’s interactive DSH Impact Calculator, which Enterprise subscribers can access through the Policy Intelligence dashboard to run custom scenarios for facilities in their markets.
